The moment the website is built, before visitors see it.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and page header
sections.what: Brings in the tools the page needs: file reading, links, navigation bar, project list, asset helper and readiness labels. The header comment explains that the list follows the refresh routine's output.
sections.why: Explains where the data comes from and why the page must stay in step with the refresh routine.
sections.watch_out: If the refresh routine in tools/clarity stops running, the list goes stale without any visible warning.

sections.name: metadata
sections.title: Page title and description
sections.what: Sets the browser title and search summary for the code index.
sections.why: Gives the page a clear name for visitors and search engines.

sections.name: loadManifest
sections.title: Reading the manifest file
sections.what: Reads the list of published explorers from the manifest file. If anything goes wrong, it returns an empty list instead.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the site still build and show a page when the file is missing.
sections.watch_out: Errors are swallowed without a message, so a broken file looks the same as having no explorers.

sections.name: CodeIndexPage
sections.title: Building the index list
sections.what: Sorts the explorers by name, shows the count and refresh date, then lists each repository with its number, link, readiness label, summary, file progress, line count, visibility and any matching project page.
sections.why: Gives visitors a clear overview before they open one explorer.
sections.watch_out: The line count is formatted directly, so an entry that has files but no lines value will fail the whole page.

summary: The Inside the code index page: it lists every published code explorer, sorted by name, with readiness, file progress and visibility for each.
purpose: Gives visitors one list of all code explorers, with a link into each one.
why: The header comment says the list must match what the refresh routine publishes, so the page reads a generated file instead of a hand-written list.
how: Step 1 reads public/code/manifest.json. Step 2 sorts the entries by name, ignoring case. Step 3 shows the title, count and refresh date. Step 4 lists each entry with its number, link, readiness label, summary, file progress, line count, visibility, and a project link when one matches.
inputs: The manifest file public/code/manifest.json, which the refresh routine in tools/clarity writes; the project data list; and the readiness label map.
outputs: A static index page with a numbered list of repositories.
risks: If the manifest is missing or broken, the page quietly shows no explorers and gives no error. An entry with files above zero but no lines value will crash the page, because the line count is formatted directly. Entries are not checked before use.
debug: First open public/code/manifest.json and confirm it is valid JSON with an entries list. Then check each entry has name, slug, readiness, files, explained, lines, visibility and mode values. The header says the file is read at build time, so rebuild the site after the manifest changes.
